summary.text: The exact adjacent-term ratios show that the weights \(\binom{n-k}{k}^L\) are geometrically concentrated near \(k=(5-\sqrt5)n/10\); on this central range, \(\binom{n+1-k}{k}/\binom{n-k}{k}=(n+1-k)/(n+1-2k)\) tends uniformly to the golden ratio, while the two tails and the endpoint correction are negligible, so the ratio of sums tends to \(\Phi^L\). Binet’s formulas identify the stated Fibonacci–Lucas expression with \(\Phi^L\), with \(L=0\) treated directly by counting the summands.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 B_{n,k}=\binom{n-k}{k}\qquad(0\leq k\leq \lfloor n/2\rfloor)
\]
and, for a nonnegative integer \(L\), let
\[
 F_L(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}B_{n,k}^{L}.
\]
We prove that
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F_L(n+1)}{F_L(n)}=\phi^L,
 \qquad \phi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\]
and then identify \(\phi^L\) with the expression involving Fibonacci and Lucas numbers.

Throughout, put
\[
 s=\sqrt5,\qquad \alpha=\frac{5-s}{10}= rac12-\frac{s}{10}.
\]
Thus \(s^2=5\), \(2<s<3\), and \(0<\alpha<1/2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Two exact ratios for the binomial summands
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The standard adjacent-binomial identities give, whenever \(2j+1\leq n\),
\[
 B_{n,j+1}(n-j)(j+1)
 =B_{n,j}(n-2j)(n-2j-1).                                      \tag{1}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 \frac{B_{n,j+1}}{B_{n,j}}
 =\frac{\binom{n-j-1}{j+1}}{\binom{n-j}{j}}
 =\frac{(n-2j)(n-2j-1)}{(n-j)(j+1)}.
\]
If \(2j=n\), then \(B_{n,j+1}=0\), so the endpoint causes no problem.

There is also an exact ratio in the \(n\)-direction. For \(2k\leq n\),
\[
 B_{n+1,k}=R_{n,k}B_{n,k},
 \qquad
 R_{n,k}:=\frac{n+1-k}{n+1-2k}.                                \tag{2}
\]
The denominator is positive. Raising (2) to the \(L\)-th power gives
\[
 B_{n+1,k}^{L}=R_{n,k}^{L}B_{n,k}^{L}.                          \tag{3}
\]

The reason for the choice of \(\alpha\) is visible in (1). If \(j\) is approximately \(xn\), the leading terms in the two factors in (1) are equal when
\[
 (1-x)x=(1-2x)^2.
\]
The root in \([0,1/2]\) is \(x=\alpha=(5-s)/10\). Thus \(B_{n,k}\) increases up to approximately \(\alpha n\) and decreases afterwards.

We record quantitative versions of this observation. They are all elementary consequences of (1). Let
\[
 P_{N,J}=(N-J)(J+1),\qquad Q_{N,J}=(N-2J)(N-2J-1).
\]
Expanding gives
\[
 P_{N,J}-Q_{N,J}
 =-5J^2+5NJ-3J-N^2+2N.                                        \tag{4}
\]
Using \(s^2=5\), one obtains the following implications for \(N\geq2\), \(J\geq0\), and \(2J\leq N\):

* if \((5-s)N\leq10J\), then \(Q_{N,J}\leq P_{N,J}\);
* if \(10J\leq(5-s)N-10\), then \(P_{N,J}\leq Q_{N,J}\).

For completeness, these signs can be seen without any approximation. In the first case,
\[
 sN-(5N-10J)\geq0.
\]
Multiplying by the nonnegative conjugate quantity \(sN+(5N-10J)\), and using \(s^2=5\), bounds the quadratic part of (4) in the required direction; the remaining linear terms have the required sign because \(N\ge2\), \(J\ge0\), and \(2J\le N\). In the second case, one applies the same calculation to
\[
 (5N-10J)-sN\geq10,
\]
where the extra \(10\) absorbs the linear terms in (4). Substitution into (4) gives exactly the two displayed inequalities.

Dividing (1) by the positive number \(P_{n,j}\), we therefore get
\[
 B_{n,j+1}\leq B_{n,j}
 \quad\hbox{if }(5-s)n\leq10j,                                 \tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 B_{n,j}\leq B_{n,j+1}
 \quad\hbox{if }10j\leq(5-s)n-10.                              \tag{6}
\]
These also hold at the last possible index, using \(B_{n,j+1}=0\) when \(2j=n\).

We also need strict geometric decay away from the transition. Let \(0<\beta\leq1\). The same expansion, now retaining the distance from the transition, gives
\[
 B_{n,j+1}\leq\left(1-\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)B_{n,j}
 \quad\text{if}\quad
 (5-s)n+10\beta n\leq10j,                                     \tag{7}
\]
and, provided \(8\leq\beta sn\),
\[
 \left(1+\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)B_{n,j}\leq B_{n,j+1}
 \quad\text{if}\quad
 10j\leq(5-s)n-10\beta n.                                    \tag{8}
\]
Here is the algebra behind these constants. Under the hypothesis of (7), multiplication of
\[
 10\beta n\leq sn-(5n-10j)
\]
by the nonnegative conjugate \(sn+(5n-10j)\), followed by \(s^2=5\), yields
\[
 \frac{\beta s}{2}n^2\leq P_{n,j}-Q_{n,j}.                    \tag{9}
\]
Since \(0<P_{n,j}\leq n^2\), (9) implies, in particular,
\[
 Q_{n,j}\leq\left(1-\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)P_{n,j};
\]
the factor \(1/4\), weaker than the \(1/2\) suggested by (9), leaves room for all endpoint and linear terms. Equation (1) then proves (7). Likewise, the hypothesis of (8), together with the same conjugate-product calculation, gives
\[
 \frac{\beta s}{2}n^2-2n\leq Q_{n,j}-P_{n,j}.                  \tag{10}
\]
The assumption \(8\leq\beta sn\) says \(2n\leq(\beta s/4)n^2\). Since \(P_{n,j}\leq n^2\), (10) gives
\[
 \left(1+\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)P_{n,j}\leq Q_{n,j},
\]
and (1) proves (8). Notice also that \(1-\beta s/4\geq0\), because \(\beta\leq1\) and \(s<3\).

Iterating (5)–(8) gives the tail estimates that will be used below. Suppose
\[
 m\geq\alpha n,\qquad m_0\leq\alpha n.
\]
Then (5) shows that \(B_{n,k}\leq B_{n,m}\) for \(m\leq k\leq n/2\), while (6) shows that \(B_{n,m_0-t}\leq B_{n,m_0}\) for \(0\leq t\leq m_0\). More quantitatively, if \(P\) is a nonnegative integer and
\[
 \alpha n+\beta n\leq m+P,
\]
then every \(k\geq m+2P\), \(k\leq n/2\), satisfies
\[
 B_{n,k}\leq
 \left(1-\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)^P B_{n,m}.                  \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, move monotonically from \(m\) to \(m+P\), and then apply (7) for at least \(P\) further steps. Similarly, if
\[
 m_0-P\leq\alpha n-\beta n,
 \qquad P\leq m_0,
 \qquad 8\leq\beta sn,
\]
then every \(k\) with \(k+2P\leq m_0\) satisfies
\[
 \left(1+\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)^P B_{n,k}\leq B_{n,m_0}.   \tag{12}
\]
This time one first uses (8) for at least \(P\) steps and then ordinary monotonicity up to \(m_0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. The ratio \(R_{n,k}\) near the central index
--------------------------------------------------------------------

A direct calculation using \(s^2=5\) and \(\phi=(1+s)/2\) gives the exact identity
\[
 R_{n,k}-\phi
 =\frac{s\bigl(k-\alpha(n+1)\bigr)}{n+1-2k}.                  \tag{13}
\]
Consequently, if
\[
 |k-\alpha(n+1)|\leq\rho,
 \qquad D\leq n+1-2k,
 \qquad D>0,
\]
then
\[
 |R_{n,k}-\phi|\leq\frac{s\rho}{D}.                           \tag{14}
\]

We shall use the following explicit central estimate. Let \(d\geq40\), \(n\geq80\), and let \(P\) satisfy
\[
 P\leq \frac nd+1.
\]
If
\[
 \alpha n-1-2P<k<\alpha n+1+2P
 \quad\text{and}\quad 2k+1\leq n,

a calculation from (14) gives
\[
 |R_{n,k}-\phi|\leq\frac{40}{n}+\frac{20}{d}.                 \tag{15}
\]
Here are the details. The interval condition implies
\[
 |k-\alpha(n+1)|\leq2+2P.
\]
Also, since \(2\alpha=1-1/s\),
\[
 n+1-2k\geq \frac{n}{2s}.
\]
To check the latter bound, use the upper bound on \(k\), then \(P\leq n/d+1\), \(d\geq40\), \(n\geq80\), and \(2<s<3\); the available main term \(n/s\) dominates the constants \(1+4P\). Thus (14) gives
\[
 |R_{n,k}-\phi|
 \leq \frac{s(2+2P)}{n/(2s)}
 =\frac{20+20P}{n}
 \leq\frac{40}{n}+\frac{20}{d},
\]
where \(s^2=5\) was used in the equality and \(P\leq n/d+1\) in the last inequality.

For positive integer \(L\), the elementary factorization of \(x^L-y^L\) yields
\[
 |x^L-y^L|
 \leq L|x-y|\max(|x|,|y|)^{L-1}.                              \tag{16}
\]
In the situation of (15), both \(R_{n,k}\) and \(\phi\) are nonnegative, \(\phi<2\), and (15) is at most \(1\); hence both are at most \(3\). Therefore
\[
 |R_{n,k}^L-\phi^L|
 \leq\left(\frac{40}{n}+\frac{20}{d}\right)L3^{L-1}.         \tag{17}
\]

Away from the central interval we use the crude estimate
\[
 |R_{n,k}^L-\phi^L|\leq2(n+1)^L.                              \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, for \(2k\leq n\), the numerator and denominator in \(R_{n,k}\) are nonnegative, and
\(0\leq R_{n,k}\leq n+1\). Also \(0<\phi<2\leq n+1\) for the values of \(n\) under consideration. Thus both \(R_{n,k}^L\) and \(\phi^L\) are at most \((n+1)^L\), proving (18).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. A quantitative bound for the ratio of the sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix a positive integer \(L\). We now prove the estimate from which the limit follows. Let \(d\geq40\), and suppose \(n\geq4d\). Put
\[
 \beta=\frac1d,
 \qquad P=\left\lfloor\frac nd\right\rfloor+1,
 \qquad m=\lceil\alpha n\rceil,
 \qquad m_0=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor,
 \qquad S=F_L(n).
\]
The elementary floor and ceiling inequalities give
\[
 \alpha n\leq m<\alpha n+1,
 \qquad
 \alpha n-1<m_0\leq\alpha n,
 \qquad
 \frac nd\leq P\leq\frac nd+1.                              \tag{19}
\]
Because \(d\geq40\), \(n\geq4d\), and \(2<s<3\), these inequalities also imply
\[
 m,m_0\leq n/2,
 \qquad P\leq m_0,
 \qquad 8\leq\beta sn.                                       \tag{20}
\]
Furthermore, (19) gives exactly the hypotheses needed in (11) and (12):
\[
 \alpha n+\beta n\leq m+P,
 \qquad
 m_0-P\leq\alpha n-\beta n.                                  \tag{21}
\]

Define the high and low tails by
\[
 H=\{k:m+2P\leq k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor\},
 \qquad
 K=\{k:0\leq k,\ k+2P\leq m_0\}.
\]
There are at most \(n+1\) terms in each. From (11), after taking \(L\)-th powers and summing,
\[
 \sum_{k\in H}B_{n,k}^L
 \leq(n+1)\left(1-\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)^{PL}B_{n,m}^L.
\]
Since the single term \(B_{n,m}^L\) is at most the whole sum \(S\),
\[
 \sum_{k\in H}B_{n,k}^L
 \leq(n+1)\left(\left(1-\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)^L\right)^P S. \tag{22}
\]
Similarly, (12) gives
\[
 \sum_{k\in K}B_{n,k}^L
 \leq(n+1)
 \left(\left(1+\frac{\beta s}{4}\right)^L\right)^{-P}S.      \tag{23}
\]
The high and low tails might overlap, but since all summands are nonnegative, the sum over their union is still bounded by the sum of the right sides of (22) and (23).

The complement of \(H\cup K\) is the central region. For every index there,
\[
 k<m+2P<\alpha n+1+2P,
 \qquad
 k+2P>m_0>\alpha n-1.
\]
Thus it lies in the interval required for (17). The harmless condition \(2k+1\leq n\) also follows from these inequalities and \(d\geq40\), \(n\geq4d\). Hence, writing
\[
 C_L=L3^{L-1},

the central contribution satisfies
\[
 \sum_{k\notin H\cup K}|R_{n,k}^L-\phi^L|B_{n,k}^L
 \leq\left(\frac{40}{n}+\frac{20}{d}\right)C_L S.            \tag{24}
\]
On the two tails, combine the crude bound (18) with (22) and (23). This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_{k\in H\cup K}|R_{n,k}^L-\phi^L|B_{n,k}^L
 \leq{}&2(n+1)^{L+1}
 \left(\left(1-\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^P S\\
 &+2(n+1)^{L+1}
 \left(\left(1+\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^{-P}S.           \tag{25}
\end{aligned}
\]

Now let
\[
 T=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}B_{n+1,k}^{L}.
\]
By (3),
\[
 T-\phi^LS
 =\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(R_{n,k}^L-\phi^L)B_{n,k}^L.
\]
Taking absolute values and using (24)–(25), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 |T-\phi^LS|\leq\Bigg[&
 \left(\frac{40}{n}+\frac{20}{d}\right)C_L\\
 &+2(n+1)^{L+1}\left(\left(1-\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^P\\
 &+2(n+1)^{L+1}\left(\left(1+\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^{-P}
 \Bigg]S.                                                     \tag{26}
\end{aligned}
\]

The only difference between \(T\) and \(F_L(n+1)\) is a possible final index. More precisely,
\[
 T\leq F_L(n+1)\leq T+1.                                     \tag{27}
\]
This follows because the ranges for \(n\) and \(n+1\) differ by at most one index, and at that possible boundary
\[
 B_{n+1,\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1}
 =\binom{n+1-(\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1)}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1}
\]
is either \(0\) or \(1\). Its \(L\)-th power is therefore at most \(1\).

Also, for \(n\geq2\),
\[
 S=F_L(n)\geq n.                                               \tag{28}
\]
Indeed, the terms \(k=0,1\) are \(1^L\) and \((n-1)^L\), and since \(L\geq1\),
\(1+(n-1)^L\geq n\).

Combining (26) and (27), dividing by the positive number \(S\), and recalling \(P=\lfloor n/d\rfloor+1\), proves the quantitative estimate
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left|\frac{F_L(n+1)}{F_L(n)}-\phi^L\right|
 \leq{}&\left(\frac{40}{n}+\frac{20}{d}\right)C_L\\
 &+2(n+1)^{L+1}
 \left(\left(1-\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^{\lfloor n/d\rfloor+1}\\
 &+2(n+1)^{L+1}
 \left(\left(1+\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^{-\lfloor n/d\rfloor-1}
 +\frac1{F_L(n)}.                                              \tag{29}
\end{aligned}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Passage to the limit when \(L\geq1\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(d\geq40\). Both exponential bases occurring in (29) lie strictly between \(0\) and \(1\):
\[
 0<\left(1-\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L<1,
 \qquad
 0<\left(\left(1+\frac{s}{4d}\right)^L\right)^{-1}<1.
\]
For every fixed \(0\leq r<1\), every fixed integer \(c\geq0\), and every positive integer \(d\),
\[
 (n+1)^c r^{\lfloor n/d\rfloor}\longrightarrow0.              \tag{30}
\]
To see this, put \(q=\lfloor n/d\rfloor\). Then \(n+1\leq d(q+1)\), so the expression is bounded by
\(d^c(q+1)^c r^q\), which tends to zero because exponential decay dominates every fixed polynomial. Thus the two tail terms in (29) tend to zero. By (28), \(1/F_L(n)\leq1/n\to0\), and of course \(40C_L/n\to0\). Consequently, for fixed \(d\), (29) gives
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}
 \left|\frac{F_L(n+1)}{F_L(n)}-\phi^L\right|
 \leq\frac{20C_L}{d}.                                        \tag{31}
\]
Finally let \(d\to\infty\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(d\geq40\) with
\(20C_L/d<\varepsilon\). For this fixed \(d\), all the remaining terms in (29) are eventually smaller than
\(\varepsilon-20C_L/d\). Hence the whole left side is eventually smaller than \(\varepsilon\). This proves
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F_L(n+1)}{F_L(n)}=\phi^L
 \qquad(L\geq1).                                               \tag{32}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. The case \(L=0\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Every summand is then \(B_{n,k}^0=1\), including when the binomial coefficient is zero, under the usual convention \(x^0=1\). Therefore
\[
 F_0(n)=\left\lfloor\frac n2\right\rfloor+1.
\]
This quantity tends to infinity and is nondecreasing, while
\[
 F_0(n)\leq F_0(n+1)\leq F_0(n)+1.
\]
After division by \(F_0(n)>0\),
\[
 1\leq\frac{F_0(n+1)}{F_0(n)}
 \leq1+\frac1{F_0(n)}.
\]
The rightmost extra term tends to zero, so by squeezing
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F_0(n+1)}{F_0(n)}=1=\phi^0.           \tag{33}
\]
Together, (32) and (33) prove the ratio limit for every nonnegative integer \(L\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Identification of the limit with Fibonacci and Lucas numbers
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let
\[
 \psi=\frac{1-s}{2}.
\]
Both \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) satisfy \(x^2=x+1\). Hence each sequence \(\phi^r\) and \(\psi^r\) satisfies
\[
 x^{r+2}=x^{r+1}+x^r.
\]
The sequence \(\phi^r+\psi^r\) has initial values \(2,1\), so by the defining recurrence of the Lucas numbers,
\[
 \operatorname{Lucas}(r)=\phi^r+\psi^r.                       \tag{34}
\]
Likewise, \((\phi^r-\psi^r)/s\) has initial values \(0,1\) and satisfies the same recurrence, so
\[
 \operatorname{Fib}(r)=\frac{\phi^r-\psi^r}{s}.               \tag{35}
\]
Using (34) and (35),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\operatorname{Fib}(L)\sqrt5+\operatorname{Lucas}(L)}2
 &=\frac{(\phi^L-\psi^L)+(\phi^L+\psi^L)}2\\
 &=\phi^L.
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this identity with (32)–(33) yields, for every nonnegative integer \(L\),
\[
 \boxed{
 \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F_L(n+1)}{F_L(n)}
 =\frac{\operatorname{Fib}(L)\sqrt5+\operatorname{Lucas}(L)}2 }.
\]
For the OEIS sequence A181546, \(L=4\), so the limit is
\(\phi^4=(7+3\sqrt5)/2\), as claimed.
